::: {.callout-important title="Provisional"}
**These numbers are provisional and the study is paused.** The packed-bed curve uses **periodic
boundary conditions**, not FoxBerry's inlet/outlet — a same-size stand-in, not a reproduction of
their case. More importantly, the campaign surfaced a **coarse-grid problem in the pressure
multigrid** that caps how far peclet can strong-scale, and the honest reading is that it should be
fixed before the ladder is re-run and published. The scaling *shape* here is a measurement of that
defect as much as of the solver.
:::

Reproduces the two 3-D strong-scaling cases of FoxBerry's `scaling/Scaling.cpp` with `peclet.flow`,
so the results drop straight onto FoxBerry's own graphs: log–log, execution time per step against
processor count, ~64M cells, the ladder 24 → 1536. Both codes are pure MPI, one rank per core, on
Snellius `genoa` nodes (192 cores each).

## What is being compared

| | FoxBerry | peclet.flow |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure solve | AMG (Trilinos/MueLu), tol 1e-14 | geometric multigrid + MG-PCG, rtol 1e-8 |
| Grid | 401³ = 64.5M | 384³ = 56.6M |
| Momentum | implicit, Chebyshev-preconditioned | implicit, Red–Black Gauss–Seidel |

The grid differs because peclet's geometric multigrid coarsens an axis only while it stays even, so
an odd dimension never coarsens at all — 401³ would cripple the pressure solve for reasons unrelated
to parallelism. Among even neighbours the *factorization* decides everything: 384 = 2⁷·3 gives seven
halvings and divides the whole rank ladder cleanly, where 400 = 2⁴·25 gives four. Measured at np=24,
384³ achieves imbalance 1.000 with all 7 levels against 400³'s 1.42 and 5. A 400³ series is kept as
a cell-count-matched control, and the gap between the two curves *is* the price of grid
factorization.

## Case 1 — single-phase flow

Unit box, inlet u=1, outlet, four no-slip walls, ρ=μ=1, 100 steps.

![](scaling_single.png)

**peclet is 8.0–9.4× faster than FoxBerry up to 384 cores, 6.0× at 1536.** The gap narrows at the
top because FoxBerry scales better: its published curve sits essentially on ideal halving across the
whole ladder, while peclet's efficiency falls to 67 % at 1536.

## Case 2 — packed bed, 5000 spheres

Same box, 5000 static spheres at solid holdup 0.45 (φ = 0.45), cut-cell IBM, D/Δ ≈ 21 cells.
**Periodic BCs and a triply-periodic bed** — same cell count, same particle count, same holdup and
sphere radius to 0.7 %, but *not* FoxBerry's boundary conditions.

![](scaling_packed.png)

**3.7–5.7× faster than FoxBerry over 24 → 384 cores.** Beyond that the pressure solve stops
converging within its iteration cap and those points are rejected as invalid rather than plotted —
384 cores is the measured ceiling of the IBM path on this problem, and the reason is the same
coarse-grid defect the callout mentions.

## Why the scaling falls off — and why it is fixable

The deficit is **not communication**. It decomposes exactly:

$$\text{speedup} \;=\; \frac{\text{per-iteration speedup}}{\text{iteration-count growth}}
\;=\; \frac{100.0\times}{2.33\times} \;=\; 42.9\times \quad (\text{single-phase, } 24 \to 1536)$$

![](scaling_diagnosis.png)

The right panel is the good news: time *per pressure iteration* improves 100× over a 64× rank
increase — **156 % efficiency, super-linear**, because the shrinking block fits cache better. The
left panel is the problem: the solve needs 2.33× more iterations at 1536 cores than at 24.

That happens because a multigrid level here coarsens an axis only if **every rank's block** is even
on it — coarse levels are required to be the fine decomposition coarsened *in place*, which keeps
the transfer operators purely local. When no axis qualifies the hierarchy simply stops. At 1536
ranks each block is 24×48×32, which stops at 3×6×4, so the hierarchy is several levels shorter than
the global grid would allow, and the preconditioner weakens accordingly.

**This is an implementation limit, not a property of multigrid**, and it is exactly what FoxBerry's
AMG does not suffer from: MueLu *repartitions its coarse levels onto fewer ranks* rather than
stopping. The standard fix is the same idea — let a coarse level live on its own coarser partition
and pay one redistribution inside the transfer, shedding ranks as the grid shrinks until the
coarsest level is solved on one. PETSc calls it `PCTELESCOPE`, MueLu `RepartitionFactory`, hypre a
redundant coarse solve, DUNE *accumulation*. peclet already has the *endpoint* of this (its
agglomerated bottom solve); what is missing is the intermediate steps.

On the packed bed the two effects compound: the starved hierarchy weakens the preconditioner enough
to push the high-contrast cut-cell operator back over its convergence threshold, which is why that
case falls off a cliff at 1536 rather than degrading gracefully. So the fix is worth more than its
33 % headline suggests — on the IBM path it plausibly buys the ability to run at all above ~400
cores.

## Reading the numbers fairly

- The 24/48/96 rungs sit on one `--exclusive` node, so they have up to 8× the memory bandwidth per
  rank of the 192-rank run. That *flatters the baseline* and therefore understates the efficiencies
  quoted above; the apples-to-apples segment is 192 → 1536 (1, 2, 4, 8 full nodes).
- 384³ is 12 % fewer cells than FoxBerry's 64.5M, and Δx is 4 % larger.
- Runs whose pressure solve hit its iteration cap on **any** step are rejected, not plotted: a
  capped step's time is set by the cap rather than by convergence.
- The bed is `peclet.dem`-grown at FoxBerry's N, holdup and radius; their PRNG is not reproducible
  outside FoxBerry, so the beds are statistically equivalent rather than identical.

## Reproducing

Everything — driver, bed generator, Snellius job scripts, result JSONs and the runbook — is in
[`benchmarks/foxberry-scaling/`](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/tree/main/benchmarks/foxberry-scaling).
The campaign's full findings, prioritized, are in the suite's `docs/SCALING_ISSUES.md`; the
coarse-grid item is written up with the standard remedies in `docs/DECOMPOSITION_AND_MULTIGRID.md`
§2.8 and open problem 1.
